properties.name: The import decision's rationale is corrected before the ruling
properties.rationale:
A DECISION IS SETTLED ON ITS RATIONALE, SO CORRECTING THE RATIONALE FIRST IS THE WHOLE POINT. Accepting it as written would embalm a false claim about this project's own history at the moment it becomes binding — and an accepted Decision is what `where-am-i` reads back to the user as "what you decided", which is where a fiction does the most damage.

THE TWO EDITS PULL IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS, and both are recorded rather than only the convenient one. Withdrawing the rename leg WEAKENS the case for reporting: that leg argued the write-time guard cannot reach the real cause, and on this graph it reaches all nine. Closing the laundering cost STRENGTHENS it: the one price the decision admitted paying is now paid down by a detector that did not exist when it was drafted.

WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT TOUCHED: the decision text itself, and the three arguments that carry it — an import ASSERTS NOTHING and reproduces a state the document is evidence of; refusal left this design's own 3388-node export unrestorable with hand-editing the export as the only remedy, which is the one thing the project tells users never to do; and `ImportReport` already answers this same question three times the other way (`skipped_edges`, `integrity_note`, `provenance_note`), so refusing here would have one import refusing what its neighbour two lines up reports. None of those three rested on the rename claim.

STATUS IS NOT MOVED BY THIS EVENT. `rule:design-intent-moves-only-on-the-owners-word` is ENFORCED and `check_intent_authority` fails the build on settled intent with no approver, so the ruling is Anthony's and is asked for separately. This only makes the thing he is ruling on true.
properties.subject: record
properties.summary: `dec:a-restore-reports-an-unresolvable-reference-rather-than-refusing-it` is about to be put to Anthony for a ruling, and its rationale contains a claim measured false the same day. Two edits, both to the rationale, none to the decision text: (1) the sentence "four capabilities renamed after the fact was written" is withdrawn and replaced with what was actually measured — those four ids never existed as nodes, so all nine of this graph's dangling values were wrong when written and every one would have been refused at write time; (2) the stated COST — "import is now a path by which a dangling reference can enter a graph that did not have one — an export/import laundering route the write guard closes" — is updated, because that route is no longer silent: the `dangling_reference` rule shipped in #373 reports an unresolvable reference on its own terms whatever the node's degree, so anything an import launders is detected on the next sweep rather than never.
